tool.name: PowerShell
tool.tagline: Cross-platform object-based shell and scripting language from Microsoft
tool.description: PowerShell is a shell and scripting language built on .NET in which commands (cmdlets) pass structured objects through the pipeline instead of text. It is the standard automation tool for Windows, Active Directory, Microsoft 365 and Azure, and PowerShell 7 runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. Learning it lets you script system administration and cloud tasks with real data types, error handling and modules.

concepts.name: Cmdlets, Get-Help and Get-Command
concepts.summary: How PowerShell commands are named, how to discover them and how to read their help.
concepts.why: Discovering commands yourself is the core PowerShell skill; everything else can be looked up.
concepts.body:
PowerShell commands are called **cmdlets** and follow a **Verb-Noun** naming pattern: `Get-Process`, `Set-Location`, `New-Item`, `Remove-Item`. The verbs come from an approved list (`Get-Verb`), so once you know the nouns you can often guess the command. Names and parameters are **case-insensitive**, and parameter names can be shortened as long as they stay unambiguous.

Three commands help you find your way:

- `Get-Command` searches commands: `Get-Command -Noun *Service*` or `Get-Command *json*`.
- `Get-Help Name -Examples` shows usage examples; `-Full` shows every parameter. Run `Update-Help` once to download the full help files, or use `-Online` to open the web page.
- `Get-Member` (next lesson) shows what an object contains.

Many cmdlets have short **aliases** such as `gci` for `Get-ChildItem`, `cd` for `Set-Location` and `%` for `ForEach-Object`. Use aliases at the prompt but full names in scripts. On Linux and macOS, aliases like `ls` and `cat` are not defined, so those names run the native programs.

Two editions exist: **Windows PowerShell 5.1** (`powershell.exe`, built into Windows, no longer developed) and **PowerShell 7** (`pwsh`, cross-platform, current). This curriculum targets PowerShell 7.5; check yours with `$PSVersionTable`.
concepts.code:
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion.ToString()   # 7.5.3
Get-Command -Noun Process              # Get-Process, Start-Process, Stop-Process, ...
Get-Command *json* -CommandType Cmdlet # ConvertFrom-Json, ConvertTo-Json, Test-Json
Get-Alias gci                          # gci -> Get-ChildItem
Get-Help Get-ChildItem -Examples       # usage examples (run Update-Help once)
Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd'          # 2026-10-17
get-date -f yyyy                       # case-insensitive, -f is short for -Format
(Get-Verb).Count                       # number of approved verbs
takeaways: Cmdlets are Verb-Noun and case-insensitive
Get-Command finds commands, Get-Help -Examples shows how to use them
Aliases at the prompt, full names in scripts
pitfalls: Using aliases like ls or cat in cross-platform scripts: on Linux they run native programs with different output.

quiz.q: You need a cmdlet that stops a Windows service but do not know its name. What is the best first step?
quiz.explain: Get-Command -Noun Service lists Get-, Start-, Stop-, Restart-Service and the rest.

quiz.q: Which executable is PowerShell 7?
quiz.explain: PowerShell 7 is pwsh; powershell.exe is the older Windows PowerShell 5.1.

concepts.name: Objects in the pipeline
concepts.summary: PowerShell pipes .NET objects with properties and methods, not text; Get-Member shows what they contain.
concepts.why: Thinking in objects instead of text columns is what makes PowerShell different from bash.
concepts.body:
In bash, commands exchange **text** and you parse it with cut, awk and regexes. In PowerShell, cmdlets output **.NET objects**, and the pipeline `|` passes those objects to the next command intact. `Get-Process` emits `Process` objects, `Get-ChildItem` emits `FileInfo` and `DirectoryInfo` objects, and so on. What you see on screen is only a formatted view chosen at the very end.

Because they are objects, you can:

- read **properties** directly: `(Get-Date).Year`, `$file.Length`,
- call **methods**: `"text".ToUpper()`, `(Get-Date).AddDays(7)`,
- sort, filter and select by property name without any parsing.

`Get-Member` (alias `gm`) is how you find out what an object offers: pipe anything into it to see its type name, properties and methods. Expect more properties than the default table shows; `Select-Object *` reveals them all.

Parentheses run a command first and let you use its result as a value: `(Get-ChildItem).Count`. When you access a property on a collection, PowerShell applies it to each element (**member enumeration**), so `(Get-Process).Name` returns every process name.

Native programs such as `git` or `ping` still output text: each line becomes a string object in the pipeline.
concepts.code:
$p = Get-Process -Id $PID                # the current PowerShell process
$p.GetType().FullName                    # System.Diagnostics.Process
$p.ProcessName                           # pwsh
$p | Get-Member -MemberType Method | Select-Object -First 2 Name
Get-ChildItem $PSHOME -File |
  Sort-Object Length -Descending |
  Select-Object -First 3 Name, Length    # properties, not text columns
(Get-Date).AddDays(7).DayOfWeek          # e.g. Saturday
'hello'.ToUpper()                        # HELLO
(1..5 | Measure-Object -Sum).Sum         # 15
(Get-ChildItem $PSHOME -File).Count      # member enumeration on a collection
takeaways: The pipeline passes objects, not text
Pipe to Get-Member to see properties and methods
(command).Property uses the result as a value
pitfalls: Parsing the formatted table output with string methods instead of using the object's properties.

quiz.q: What travels between `Get-ChildItem | Sort-Object Length`?
quiz.explain: Cmdlets pass .NET objects; Sort-Object reads their Length property directly.

quiz.q: Which command shows the properties and methods of an object?
quiz.explain: Get-Member lists the type, properties and methods of whatever is piped into it.

concepts.name: Variables, types and strings
concepts.summary: Store values in $variables, understand type conversion and expand variables in double-quoted strings.
concepts.why: Variables and string expansion appear on nearly every line of a PowerShell script.
concepts.body:
Variables start with `$` and are created on assignment: `$name = 'Ada'`. Spaces around `=` are fine. Names are case-insensitive. Values keep their **.NET type**: `$count = 3` is an `Int32`, `3.5` a `Double`, `'x'` a `String`, `$true` a `Boolean`; `$null` means nothing.

Strings come in two flavours:

- **Double quotes** expand variables: `"Hello $name"`. For anything more than a plain variable, such as a property or an expression, use a **subexpression** `$( )`: `"Files: $($files.Count)"`.
- **Single quotes** are literal: `'Cost: $5'`.

The escape character is the **backtick** (`` `n `` newline, `` `t `` tab), not the backslash, which is just a normal character, convenient for Windows paths.

PowerShell converts types automatically, and **the left operand decides**: `'42' + 1` gives the string `421`, while `1 + '42'` gives `43`. Cast explicitly with `[int]'42'`. Putting a type before a variable at assignment, `[int]$age = '30'`, constrains it, and later assignments must also convert to int.

Environment variables live in the `env:` drive: `$env:PATH`, `$env:HOME`. Automatic variables include `$PSVersionTable`, `$PID`, `$HOME`, `$true`, `$false` and `$null`. When comparing with `$null`, put it on the left: `$null -eq $x`.
concepts.code:
$name = 'Ada'
$count = 3
"Hello $name, you have $count new messages"   # expands variables
'Hello $name'                     # Hello $name  (single quotes: literal)
"Total: $($count * 2)"            # Total: 6     ($() for expressions)
"Tab:`tdone"                      # Tab:    done (backtick escapes)
$count.GetType().Name             # Int32
'42' + 1                          # 421  (left operand is a string)
1 + '42'                          # 43
[int]'42' + 1                     # 43
[int]$age = '30'                  # constrained to int
$age.GetType().Name               # Int32
# $age = 'thirty'                 # error: cannot convert value "thirty" to type "System.Int32"
$null -eq $undefinedVariable      # True
$env:HOME                         # /home/you  (environment variable)
takeaways: Double quotes expand $var and $(expr); single quotes are literal
The left operand's type drives conversion: '42' + 1 is '421'
Backtick is the escape character; $env:NAME reads environment variables
pitfalls: Writing "Size: $file.Length" and getting the whole object followed by '.Length'; use $($file.Length).

quiz.q: What does `'5' + 5` return?
quiz.explain: The left operand is a string, so + concatenates and 5 is converted to '5'.

quiz.q: With $f = Get-Item ./a.txt, which string shows the file size correctly?
quiz.explain: Only a subexpression inside double quotes evaluates the property access.

concepts.name: Filter, sort and select
concepts.summary: Shape pipeline output with Where-Object, Sort-Object, Select-Object, Group-Object and Measure-Object.
concepts.why: These five cmdlets answer most 'which ones, how many, the biggest' questions about any data.
concepts.body:
Once data is objects, a handful of cmdlets do most of the work:

- **Where-Object** filters: `Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 1MB }`. Inside the script block, `$_` (or `$PSItem`) is the current object. For a single comparison the simplified form `Where-Object Length -gt 1MB` also works.
- **Sort-Object** orders by one or more properties: `Sort-Object Length -Descending`.
- **Select-Object** picks properties (`Select-Object Name, Length`), takes `-First`/`-Last` items, removes duplicates with `-Unique`, and `-ExpandProperty Name` returns the bare values instead of objects with one property.
- **Group-Object** groups by a property and counts.
- **Measure-Object** computes count, sum, average, minimum and maximum.

**Calculated properties** add or rename columns: `@{ Name = 'KB'; Expression = { $_.Length / 1KB } }`. Size suffixes `KB`, `MB`, `GB` are built-in numeric literals.

**Filter left**: when a cmdlet has its own filter parameter, such as `Get-ChildItem -Filter *.log` or `Get-Process -Name pwsh`, use it. The provider or API does the filtering before objects are created, which can be dramatically faster than `Where-Object` on large sets, especially against remote systems.
concepts.code:
$files = Get-ChildItem $PSHOME -File
$files | Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 1MB } | Measure-Object |
  Select-Object -ExpandProperty Count            # how many files > 1 MB
$files | Where-Object Extension -eq '.json' |
  Select-Object -First 2 -ExpandProperty Name    # simplified syntax
$files | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 3 Name,
  @{ Name = 'KB'; Expression = { [math]::Round($_.Length / 1KB) } }
$files | Group-Object Extension | Sort-Object Count -Descending |
  Select-Object -First 3 Count, Name             # most common extensions
$files | Measure-Object Length -Sum -Maximum | Select-Object Count, Sum, Maximum
Get-ChildItem $PSHOME -Filter *.json             # filter left: provider does it
takeaways: Where-Object filters, Sort-Object orders, Select-Object picks
$_ is the current object inside script blocks
Use a cmdlet's own -Filter or -Name parameter before Where-Object
pitfalls: Expecting `Select-Object Name` to return strings; it returns objects with a Name property. Use -ExpandProperty.

quiz.q: Which command returns plain strings of process names?
quiz.explain: -ExpandProperty unwraps the property value; plain Select-Object keeps objects with one property.

quiz.q: Why prefer `Get-ChildItem -Filter *.log` over piping to `Where-Object Name -like '*.log'`?
options: It filters before objects are created, so it is faster
quiz.explain: Filtering at the source avoids building and piping objects you would throw away.

concepts.name: Files, paths and providers
concepts.summary: Navigate, read, write, copy and delete files, build paths safely and use drives such as Env:.
concepts.why: Most automation reads or writes files, and providers let the same cmdlets reach other data stores.
concepts.body:
File work uses a small, consistent set of cmdlets: `Get-ChildItem` (list), `Set-Location` (cd), `New-Item`, `Copy-Item`, `Move-Item`, `Rename-Item`, `Remove-Item`, `Test-Path`. Their `-Path` parameter accepts wildcards; use `-LiteralPath` for names that contain `[` or `]`. `-Recurse` walks subdirectories, and `-Force` includes hidden items or overwrites.

Reading and writing text:

- `Get-Content file` returns an **array of lines**; add `-Raw` for a single string.
- `Set-Content` replaces a file, `Add-Content` appends, `Out-File` writes formatted output.
- In PowerShell 7 the default encoding is UTF-8 without a BOM; specify `-Encoding` when a tool expects something else.

Build paths with `Join-Path` and `Split-Path` instead of string concatenation; on Linux the separator is `/`, and both cmdlets handle it.

Destructive cmdlets support `-WhatIf` (show what would happen) and `-Confirm` (ask first): run `Remove-Item -Recurse -WhatIf` before the real thing.

The same cmdlets work on other **providers**, exposed as drives: `Env:` (environment variables), `Variable:`, `Function:`, `Alias:`, and on Windows `HKLM:` (the registry) and `Cert:` (certificates). `Get-PSDrive` lists them, so `Get-ChildItem Env:` lists environment variables just like files.
concepts.code:
$dir = Join-Path ([IO.Path]::GetTempPath()) 'ps-demo'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $dir -Force | Out-Null
Set-Location $dir
Set-Content -Path notes.txt -Value 'first line'
Add-Content -Path notes.txt -Value 'second line'
Get-Content notes.txt                 # first line / second line
(Get-Content notes.txt).Count         # 2   (an array of lines)
Copy-Item notes.txt backup.txt
Test-Path backup.txt                  # True
Get-ChildItem -Filter *.txt | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name   # backup.txt notes.txt
Remove-Item backup.txt -WhatIf        # What if: Performing the operation "Remove File" ...
Split-Path (Join-Path $dir 'notes.txt') -Leaf   # notes.txt
Get-ChildItem Env: | Select-Object -First 2 Name   # environment as a drive
takeaways: Get-ChildItem, Copy-Item, Remove-Item and friends work on any provider
Get-Content returns lines; -Raw returns one string
Join-Path for paths, -WhatIf before destructive commands
pitfalls: Concatenating paths with '\' in scripts that must also run on Linux or macOS.

quiz.q: What does `Get-Content log.txt` return for a 3-line file?
quiz.explain: Get-Content emits one string per line; use -Raw to get a single string.

quiz.q: What is `-WhatIf` for?
options: Showing what a command would do without doing it
Running a command only if a condition is true
quiz.explain: -WhatIf describes the operation instead of performing it.

concepts.name: Operators, if, switch and loops
concepts.summary: Compare with -eq, -like and -match, branch with if and switch, and loop with foreach, for and while.
concepts.why: PowerShell's dash-style operators and case-insensitive defaults trip up everyone coming from other languages.
concepts.body:
Comparison operators are words with a dash, because `>` and `<` are redirection: `-eq -ne -gt -ge -lt -le`. String operators: `-like` (wildcards `*` and `?`), `-match` (regex, fills the automatic `$Matches` variable), `-replace` (regex replace). Membership: `-contains` (collection on the left) and `-in` (collection on the right). All are **case-insensitive** by default; prefix with `c` for case-sensitive: `-ceq`, `-cmatch`.

A surprise: with a **collection on the left**, comparison operators filter instead of returning a boolean. `1, 5, 9 -gt 4` returns `5, 9`. That is why `$null -eq $x` is written with `$null` first.

Branching: `if (...) { } elseif (...) { } else { }`. `switch` matches a value against cases and supports `-Wildcard`, `-Regex` and script-block conditions. Unlike C, **every** matching case runs unless you `break`, and given an array, switch processes each element.

Loops:

- `foreach ($item in $collection) { }` statement: fast, for data already in memory,
- `ForEach-Object { $_ }` cmdlet: streams pipeline input one item at a time,
- `for ($i = 0; $i -lt 10; $i++) { }`, `while`, `do { } while/until`.

`1..5` is a range, and logical operators are `-and`, `-or`, `-not` (or `!`).
concepts.code:
$n = 7
if ($n -gt 5) { 'big' } elseif ($n -gt 2) { 'medium' } else { 'small' }   # big
'Hello' -eq 'hello'               # True   (case-insensitive by default)
'Hello' -ceq 'hello'              # False
'report.csv' -like '*.csv'        # True
'v2.15' -match 'v(\d+)\.(\d+)'    # True
$Matches[1]                       # 2
'b' -in 'a', 'b', 'c'             # True
1, 5, 9 -gt 4                     # 5 / 9   (a collection on the left filters!)
switch -Wildcard ('error.log') {
  '*.log' { 'log file' }          # log file
  'err*'  { 'error-ish' }         # error-ish  (every matching case runs)
}
foreach ($i in 1..3) { "item $i" }      # item 1 / item 2 / item 3
$i = 0; while ($i -lt 3) { $i++ }; $i   # 3
takeaways: -eq -gt -like -match: case-insensitive unless prefixed with c
A collection on the left of a comparison filters it
switch runs every matching case; foreach statement vs ForEach-Object cmdlet
pitfalls: Writing `if ($x > 5)`: > is redirection and creates a file named 5.

quiz.q: What does `if ($count > 10) { ... }` actually do?
quiz.explain: In PowerShell > is the redirection operator; use -gt for comparisons.

quiz.q: What does `'a','b','a' -eq 'a'` return?
quiz.explain: With a collection on the left, -eq returns the matching elements.

concepts.name: Arrays and hashtables
concepts.summary: Create and use arrays, generic lists, hashtables and ordered dictionaries.
concepts.why: Collections and key/value maps hold the data of every non-trivial script.
concepts.body:
**Arrays** are created with commas or `@( )`: `$a = 1, 2, 3` or `$a = @('x', 'y')`. Index from 0 and from the end with negatives: `$a[0]`, `$a[-1]`; slices with ranges: `$a[0..1]`. `$a.Count` gives the length. Arrays are **fixed-size**: `$a += 4` builds a whole new array each time, which is fine for a handful of items and slow for thousands. For growing collections use `[System.Collections.Generic.List[object]]` (or a typed `List[string]`) and `.Add()`.

`@( ... )` around a command **guarantees an array**, even when the command returns zero or one item, so `.Count` and indexing always behave.

**Hashtables** map keys to values: `$h = @{ Name = 'Ada'; Role = 'admin' }`. Read with `$h.Name` or `$h['Name']`, add by assigning a new key, test with `.ContainsKey()`, remove with `.Remove()`. Keys are case-insensitive by default. A plain hashtable does not keep insertion order; `[ordered]@{ }` does, which matters for output and JSON.

To loop over a hashtable, iterate `$h.GetEnumerator()` (giving `.Key` and `.Value`) or `$h.Keys`. Hashtables are also used for **splatting**: `$params = @{ Path = '.'; Recurse = $true }; Get-ChildItem @params` passes keys as named parameters, which keeps long commands readable.
concepts.code:
$fruits = @('apple', 'banana')
$fruits += 'cherry'                   # creates a NEW array
$fruits[0]; $fruits[-1]               # apple / cherry
$fruits.Count                         # 3
$fruits -contains 'kiwi'              # False
$list = [System.Collections.Generic.List[string]]::new()
$list.Add('fast'); $list.Count        # 1   (use for big, growing lists)
$user = @{ Name = 'Ada'; Role = 'admin' }
$user.Name                            # Ada
$user['role']                         # admin  (keys are case-insensitive)
$user.Email = 'ada@example.com'       # add a key
$user.ContainsKey('Email')            # True
$ordered = [ordered]@{ b = 2; a = 1 }
$ordered.Keys -join ','               # b,a   (insertion order kept)
foreach ($kv in $ordered.GetEnumerator()) { "$($kv.Key)=$($kv.Value)" }   # b=2 / a=1
$params = @{ Path = $PSHOME; Filter = '*.json' }
@(Get-ChildItem @params).Count -gt 0  # True   (splatting + @() for an array)
takeaways: Arrays: 1, 2, 3 or @(); += copies, use List[T] for growth
@{ } hashtable, [ordered]@{ } keeps key order
Splat a hashtable of parameters with @params
pitfalls: Building a large result with `$results += $item` in a loop: it is quadratic.

quiz.q: A command returns a single string 'abc'. What is `$r[0]` without @() and `@($r)[0]` with it?
quiz.explain: Indexing a lone string returns a character; @() wraps the result in an array so [0] is the whole item.

quiz.q: What does `Get-ChildItem @opts` do when $opts is a hashtable?
options: Passes each key/value as a named parameter
Passes the hashtable as one argument
quiz.explain: Splatting expands the hashtable's keys into parameter names and values.

concepts.name: Functions and parameters
concepts.summary: Write functions with typed, mandatory, validated and switch parameters, and call them the PowerShell way.
concepts.why: Functions with proper parameters behave like real cmdlets: tab completion, validation and help for free.
concepts.body:
Define a function with `function Verb-Noun { param(...) ... }`. Use an approved verb so it fits in with the built-in commands. The `param()` block declares parameters:

- a **type** like `[string]` or `[int]` converts and validates the input,
- a **default value**: `[string]$Word = 'Hello'`,
- `[Parameter(Mandatory)]` prompts if the value is missing (or fails in non-interactive runs),
- validation attributes: `[ValidateSet('a','b')]`, `[ValidateRange(1,10)]`, `[ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]`, `[ValidatePattern('^\d+$')]`,
- `[switch]$Force` is an on/off flag that is `$true` when present.

**Calling** works like any cmdlet: `Get-Greeting -Name Ada -Shout`, or positionally `Get-Greeting Ada`. Never call with parentheses and commas: `Add(2, 3)` passes a **single array** to the first parameter. Parentheses and commas are only for .NET methods.

What a function **returns** is everything it outputs: any value not assigned or discarded goes to the pipeline. `return $x` just outputs `$x` and exits. Discard unwanted output with `$null = ...` or `| Out-Null`.

Tab completion works for your parameters, and a comment-based help block (`<# .SYNOPSIS ... #>`) makes `Get-Help` work for your function.
concepts.code:
function Get-Greeting {
  param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory)]
    [string]$Name,
    [ValidateSet('Hello', 'Hi', 'Welcome')]
    [string]$Word = 'Hello',
    [switch]$Shout
  )
  $text = "$Word, $Name!"
  if ($Shout) { $text = $text.ToUpper() }
  $text                              # output = return value
}
Get-Greeting -Name Ada               # Hello, Ada!
Get-Greeting Bob -Word Hi -Shout     # HI, BOB!
# Get-Greeting -Name Cy -Word Yo     # error: "Yo" does not belong to the set
function Add-Numbers($a, $b) { $a + $b }
Add-Numbers 2 3                      # 5      (spaces, no commas)
Add-Numbers(2, 3)                    # 2 / 3  ($a got the array 2,3; $b is empty)
takeaways: param() with types, defaults, Mandatory, Validate* and [switch]
Call functions like cmdlets: Name -Param value, no parentheses or commas
Every uncaptured value is output; return just exits
pitfalls: Calling `MyFunc($a, $b)` like a method, which passes one array argument.

quiz.q: How do you call a function `Add-Numbers($a, $b)` with 2 and 3?
quiz.explain: Arguments are space-separated; a comma makes an array.

quiz.q: What is the value of a [switch]$Force parameter when the caller omits -Force?
quiz.explain: A switch is false unless the flag is supplied.

concepts.name: Scripts, execution policy and profiles
concepts.summary: Write .ps1 scripts with a param block, run them on any OS, and understand execution policy, dot-sourcing and $PROFILE.
concepts.why: Saving work as scripts is how ad-hoc commands become repeatable automation.
concepts.body:
A script is a `.ps1` file. It can start with a `param()` block, exactly like a function, so it gets named parameters, validation and tab completion. Run it with its path, `./backup.ps1 -Source ./docs`, or from another shell with `pwsh -File ./backup.ps1`. On Linux and macOS a `#!/usr/bin/env pwsh` shebang plus `chmod +x` also works.

Useful automatic variables: `$PSScriptRoot` is the folder containing the script, the reliable base for relative paths; `$PSCommandPath` is the script's full path. `#Requires -Version 7.0` or `#Requires -Modules Name` stop the script early if requirements are missing. `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` turns references to undefined variables and properties into errors.

**Execution policy** applies on Windows only: it controls whether scripts may run (`Restricted`, `RemoteSigned`, `AllSigned`, `Unrestricted`, `Bypass`). Check it with `Get-ExecutionPolicy -List`; developers typically use `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned`. Downloaded files are marked and may need `Unblock-File`. It is a safety feature against accidents, **not a security boundary**.

**Dot-sourcing** `. ./helpers.ps1` runs a script in the current scope so its functions and variables remain available. Your **profile**, at the path in `$PROFILE`, is dot-sourced at startup; put aliases, functions and prompt tweaks there.
concepts.code:
# file: backup.ps1
#Requires -Version 7.0
param(
  [Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Source,
  [string]$Destination = (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'backups')
)
Set-StrictMode -Version Latest
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $Destination -Force | Out-Null
$stamp = Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMdd-HHmmss'
Compress-Archive -Path $Source -DestinationPath "$Destination/backup-$stamp.zip"
"Saved to $Destination"
# Running it:
#   ./backup.ps1 -Source ./docs
#   pwsh -File ./backup.ps1 -Source ./docs      (from bash, cmd, cron...)
# Windows only:
#   Get-ExecutionPolicy -List
#   Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned
# . ./helpers.ps1    # dot-source: load its functions into this scope
# $PROFILE           # path of your startup profile script
takeaways: A param() block at the top makes a script take named parameters
$PSScriptRoot anchors relative paths
Execution policy is a Windows safety setting, not security; dot-source to import
pitfalls: Using relative paths that depend on the caller's current directory instead of $PSScriptRoot.

quiz.q: A script reads './config.json' and fails when run from another folder. What is the fix?
quiz.explain: Relative paths resolve against the current location; $PSScriptRoot is the script's own folder.

quiz.q: What does dot-sourcing `. ./lib.ps1` do?
options: Runs lib.ps1 in a child scope
Runs it in the current scope so its definitions remain
quiz.explain: Dot-sourcing keeps the functions and variables lib.ps1 defines in the caller's scope.

concepts.name: Output, formatting and Write-Host
concepts.summary: Know the difference between output and display: Write-Output, Write-Host, Write-Verbose, Format-* and Out-*.
concepts.why: Mixing up output and display is the top reason PowerShell functions return garbage or print nothing.
concepts.body:
PowerShell separates **output** (objects sent down the pipeline, which callers can capture) from **display** (what the host shows you). Anything not captured is output; `Write-Output` is the explicit form but rarely needed.

For messages, use the cmdlet for the purpose, because each writes to its own stream, not to the output:

- `Write-Verbose` (shown with `-Verbose`), `Write-Debug`, `Write-Warning`, `Write-Error`,
- `Write-Information` and `Write-Host` for user-facing text; `Write-Host` can add colour.

That way `$result = My-Function` captures only data, not chatter.

**Format-Table**, **Format-List** and **Format-Wide** turn objects into formatting instructions for display. Use them only at the **end** of a pipeline: after `Format-Table` you no longer have the original objects, so sorting, exporting or reading properties breaks. To get text, use `Out-String`; to write to a file, `Out-File` or `Set-Content`; to save data, prefer `Export-Csv` or `ConvertTo-Json`.

The `-f` format operator builds strings: `'{0} is {1:N1} GB' -f $name, $size`, with .NET format codes like `N2`, `P0` (percent) and `yyyy-MM-dd` for dates. `Out-Null` or `$null = ...` discard output you do not want.
concepts.code:
function Get-Info {
  [CmdletBinding()] param()
  Write-Verbose 'collecting'                  # only shown with -Verbose
  Write-Host 'progress...' -ForegroundColor Cyan   # display, not output
  [pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'disk'; UsedGB = 41.53 }
}
$r = Get-Info                                 # screen shows: progress...
$r.UsedGB                                     # 41.53  (the object was captured)
Get-Info -Verbose | Out-Null                  # VERBOSE: collecting
Get-ChildItem $PSHOME -File | Select-Object -First 3 Name, Length |
  Format-Table -AutoSize                      # display only, at the very end
'{0} is {1:N1} GB' -f 'disk', 41.53           # disk is 41.5 GB
$text = Get-Process -Id $PID | Out-String     # render as one string
$text.GetType().Name                          # String
takeaways: Output goes down the pipeline; Write-Host only displays
Write-Verbose / Warning / Error keep messages out of captured data
Format-* only at the end; Out-String, Export-Csv or ConvertTo-Json for data
pitfalls: `Get-Process | Format-Table | Export-Csv`: the CSV contains formatting objects, not processes.

quiz.q: A function prints a message with Write-Output and returns a number. What does `$x = Func` contain?
quiz.explain: Write-Output sends to the output stream, so both values are captured; use Write-Verbose or Write-Host for messages.

quiz.q: Where should Format-Table appear in a pipeline?
quiz.explain: Format cmdlets produce display instructions; later commands cannot use the original objects.

concepts.name: Custom objects, JSON and CSV
concepts.summary: Create [pscustomobject] records and move data in and out of JSON, CSV and REST APIs.
concepts.why: Real scripts read data from files and APIs, reshape it and write reports.
concepts.body:
`[pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'web1'; CPU = 72 }` creates an object with those properties, in that order. Custom objects flow through the pipeline like any cmdlet output: you can filter, sort, group and export them. They are the right way to return structured results from your functions, instead of formatted strings.

**JSON**: `ConvertTo-Json` serializes objects (mind `-Depth`: the default of 2 truncates deeper nesting, with a warning), and `ConvertFrom-Json` parses text into objects; `-AsHashtable` gives hashtables instead. Read a file with `Get-Content file.json -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json`.

**CSV**: `Export-Csv` writes objects (PowerShell 7 no longer adds a type header, so `-NoTypeInformation` is optional), and `Import-Csv` reads rows back as objects whose property values are **all strings**. Cast before comparing numbers: `[int]$_.CPU -gt 50`.

**REST**: `Invoke-RestMethod` calls an HTTP API and converts the JSON response into objects automatically; `Invoke-WebRequest` gives the raw response with status code and headers.

To add a property to an existing object use `Add-Member` or `Select-Object *, @{ Name = 'New'; Expression = { ... } }`. `ForEach-Object Name` (member name shorthand) pulls a single property out of each object.
concepts.code:
Set-Location ([IO.Path]::GetTempPath())
$servers = @(
  [pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'web1'; CPU = 72; Env = 'prod' }
  [pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'web2'; CPU = 15; Env = 'prod' }
  [pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'dev1'; CPU = 90; Env = 'dev' }
)
$servers | Where-Object CPU -gt 50 | ForEach-Object Name   # web1 / dev1
$json = $servers | ConvertTo-Json -Compress
$json.Substring(0, 38)              # [{"Name":"web1","CPU":72,"Env":"prod"}
$back = $json | ConvertFrom-Json
$back[2].CPU + 1                    # 91
$servers | Export-Csv servers.csv
(Import-Csv servers.csv)[0].CPU.GetType().Name     # String  (CSV is text)
@(Import-Csv servers.csv | Where-Object { [int]$_.CPU -gt 50 }).Count   # 2
$servers | Group-Object Env | ForEach-Object { "$($_.Name): $($_.Count)" }   # dev: 1 / prod: 2  (groups sorted by name)
# $repo = Invoke-RestMethod https://api.github.com/repos/PowerShell/PowerShell
# $repo.stargazers_count          # JSON response arrives as objects
takeaways: [pscustomobject]@{ } is the standard record type
ConvertTo-Json needs -Depth for nested data
Import-Csv values are strings; cast before numeric comparisons
pitfalls: Comparing Import-Csv values as numbers without casting: '9' -gt '50' is True as strings.

quiz.q: After Import-Csv, `$row.Count -gt 100` behaves oddly. Why?
options: CSV values are strings, so the comparison is textual
quiz.explain: Every imported value is a string; cast with [int] to compare numerically.

quiz.q: What can go wrong with `$deep | ConvertTo-Json` on nested data?
options: Levels beyond the default depth of 2 are truncated to strings
quiz.explain: Raise -Depth to serialize deeper structures fully.

concepts.name: Error handling: try/catch and -ErrorAction
concepts.summary: Terminating vs non-terminating errors, -ErrorAction Stop, try/catch/finally, $ErrorActionPreference and native exit codes.
concepts.why: Without understanding the two kinds of errors, try/catch silently fails to catch most cmdlet errors.
concepts.body:
PowerShell has two kinds of errors:

- **Non-terminating** errors, the default for most cmdlets: the error is reported (and added to `$Error`) but the command continues with the next item. `try/catch` does **not** see these.
- **Terminating** errors: `throw`, .NET exceptions, and any error raised with `-ErrorAction Stop`. These stop the current statement and can be caught.

So the standard pattern is `try { Some-Cmdlet -ErrorAction Stop } catch { ... }`. Inside `catch`, `$_` is the **ErrorRecord**: `$_.Exception.Message`, `$_.Exception.GetType()`, `$_.TargetObject`, `$_.InvocationInfo.ScriptLineNumber`. You can catch specific exception types first and a general `catch` last. `finally` always runs, for cleanup.

`-ErrorAction` (common parameter) per call: `Stop`, `Continue` (default), `SilentlyContinue`, `Ignore`. `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` at the top of a script makes all cmdlet errors terminating, which is the PowerShell equivalent of bash's `set -e`. `-ErrorVariable errs` collects a call's errors into a variable.

**Native programs** (git, docker) do not throw; check `$LASTEXITCODE` after them, or in 7.4+ set `$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true` so a non-zero exit becomes an error. `$?` tells whether the last command succeeded.
takeaways: try/catch only sees terminating errors; add -ErrorAction Stop
$_ in catch is the ErrorRecord; finally always runs
Check $LASTEXITCODE after native programs
pitfalls: Wrapping a cmdlet in try/catch without -ErrorAction Stop and wondering why catch never runs.

quiz.q: `try { Remove-Item missing.txt } catch { 'oops' }` prints an error but not 'oops'. Why?
options: Remove-Item's error is non-terminating; add -ErrorAction Stop
quiz.explain: Most cmdlet errors are non-terminating and bypass catch unless made terminating.

quiz.q: How do you detect that `git push` failed in a script?
quiz.explain: Native programs report failure through their exit code, stored in $LASTEXITCODE.

concepts.name: Advanced functions and pipeline input
concepts.summary: Use [CmdletBinding()], begin/process/end blocks and ValueFromPipeline to write functions that act like real cmdlets.
concepts.why: Pipeline-aware functions compose with built-in cmdlets and stream large inputs efficiently.
concepts.body:
Adding `[CmdletBinding()]` above `param()` turns a function into an **advanced function**. It gains the common parameters (`-Verbose`, `-ErrorAction`, `-WhatIf` when declared...) and the `$PSCmdlet` object.

To accept **pipeline input**, mark a parameter with `ValueFromPipeline` (the whole object binds) or `ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName` (a property with the same name, or an `[Alias()]`, binds). The function body is then split into blocks:

- `begin { }` runs once before the first item: initialise counters, open connections,
- `process { }` runs **once per pipeline item**, with the parameter bound to that item,
- `end { }` runs once at the end: totals, cleanup.

Without a `process` block the whole body acts like `end` and only sees the last item. Declare array parameters (`[string[]]`) and loop inside `process`, so the function works both when piped and when called with several values directly.

For commands that change things, add `[CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess)]` and guard changes with `if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($target, 'Delete')) { ... }`. Your function then supports `-WhatIf` and `-Confirm` automatically, just like `Remove-Item`. Emit objects with `[pscustomobject]` rather than formatted text so callers can keep piping.
takeaways: [CmdletBinding()] adds common parameters like -Verbose
ValueFromPipeline / ByPropertyName bind piped objects
begin once, process per item, end once; SupportsShouldProcess adds -WhatIf
pitfalls: Omitting the process block, so a piped function only handles the last item.

quiz.q: A pipeline-aware function has no begin/process/end blocks. What does it see when 5 items are piped in?
options: All 5 items one at a time
quiz.explain: Without explicit blocks the body runs as end, after the pipeline, with the last bound value.

quiz.q: What does SupportsShouldProcess give your function?
quiz.explain: Combined with $PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess(), it makes -WhatIf and -Confirm work.

concepts.name: Modules and the PowerShell Gallery
concepts.summary: Install modules from the PowerShell Gallery and package your own functions as a module with a manifest.
concepts.why: Modules are how PowerShell code is shared, versioned and reused across scripts and teams.
concepts.body:
A **module** is a package of commands. Most of PowerShell itself ships as modules, and thousands more (Az for Azure, Pester for testing, PSScriptAnalyzer for linting, Microsoft.Graph) are published on the **PowerShell Gallery**.

In PowerShell 7.4+ the **PSResourceGet** cmdlets manage them: `Find-PSResource`, `Install-PSResource -Scope CurrentUser`, `Update-PSResource`. The older PowerShellGet commands (`Install-Module`) still work. Modules are found in the folders listed in `$env:PSModulePath` and **auto-loaded** the first time you use one of their commands, so `Import-Module` is mostly needed for modules outside those folders or to reload with `-Force` during development.

Your own **script module** is a `.psm1` file with functions; put it in a folder of the same name. Control what is public with `Export-ModuleMember` or, better, a **manifest** (`.psd1`) created by `New-ModuleManifest`, which declares the version, author, dependencies and `FunctionsToExport`. Explicit exports keep helper functions private and make auto-loading fast.

Common layout: one function per `.ps1` file in `Public/` and `Private/` folders, dot-sourced by the `.psm1`, plus Pester tests. `Get-Command -Module Name` lists a module's commands and `Get-Module` shows what is loaded.
concepts.code:
Find-PSResource -Name Pester                        # search the PowerShell Gallery
Install-PSResource -Name Pester -Scope CurrentUser  # PSResourceGet (7.4+)
Get-Module -ListAvailable Pester | Select-Object Name, Version
# Your own module: MyTools/MyTools.psm1
#   function Get-Answer { Get-InternalValue }
#   function Get-InternalValue { 42 }               # helper, kept private
New-ModuleManifest ./MyTools/MyTools.psd1 -RootModule MyTools.psm1 `
  -ModuleVersion 1.0.0 -FunctionsToExport Get-Answer
Import-Module ./MyTools -Force
Get-Answer                                          # 42
Get-Command -Module MyTools | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name   # Get-Answer
Get-InternalValue                                   # error: not recognized (private)
$env:PSModulePath -split [IO.Path]::PathSeparator   # where modules are discovered
takeaways: Install-PSResource gets modules from the PowerShell Gallery
Modules on $env:PSModulePath auto-load on first use
A .psd1 manifest declares version and exported functions
pitfalls: Exporting every function with wildcards, which exposes helpers and slows auto-loading.

quiz.q: Why is Import-Module often unnecessary?
options: Modules on PSModulePath auto-load when you first use a command
quiz.explain: Command discovery auto-imports modules found in PSModulePath.

quiz.q: What does FunctionsToExport in a module manifest control?
options: Which functions callers can see after import
quiz.explain: Only the listed functions are public; the rest stay internal to the module.

concepts.name: Jobs, parallelism and remoting
concepts.summary: Run work concurrently with Start-ThreadJob and ForEach-Object -Parallel, and on other machines with Invoke-Command.
concepts.why: Parallel and remote execution turn slow, one-machine-at-a-time scripts into fleet automation.
concepts.body:
PowerShell has several ways to run work concurrently:

- **Start-Job** runs a script block in a separate background **process**. Isolated but heavy (a new pwsh starts each time).
- **Start-ThreadJob** runs it on a **thread** in the same process: much lighter, the usual choice. Both return job objects; collect results with `Receive-Job` (`-Wait` to block) and clean up with `Remove-Job`.
- **ForEach-Object -Parallel** (PowerShell 7) processes pipeline items concurrently in runspaces, with `-ThrottleLimit` (default 5) capping concurrency.

Code in a job or a parallel block cannot see your variables. Pass values with the **`$using:`** scope modifier, which copies them in: `$using:token`. Do not modify shared collections from parallel blocks; output results and collect them instead.

Parallelism pays off for I/O-bound work like web calls, remote commands and file copies. For tiny CPU tasks, the overhead of runspaces can make it slower than a plain loop.

**Remoting** runs commands on other machines: `Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv1, srv2 -ScriptBlock { ... }` executes in parallel on all of them over WinRM (Windows), and `-HostName` uses **SSH**, which works cross-platform. `Enter-PSSession` gives an interactive remote prompt; `New-PSSession` keeps a reusable connection. Results come back as deserialized objects (properties only, no methods).
takeaways: Start-ThreadJob is light, Start-Job isolates in a process
ForEach-Object -Parallel with -ThrottleLimit for concurrent pipelines
$using:var passes local values into jobs, parallel blocks and remote sessions
pitfalls: Referencing $myVar inside -Parallel or a job without $using: and getting $null.

quiz.q: Inside ForEach-Object -Parallel, how do you read the caller's $limit variable?
quiz.explain: Each parallel runspace is isolated; $using: copies the caller's value in.

quiz.q: Which is the lightest way to run a background task in PowerShell 7?
quiz.explain: Thread jobs run in the same process, avoiding the cost of starting a new pwsh.

concepts.name: Using .NET and PowerShell classes
concepts.summary: Call any .NET API with [Type]::Method(), create objects with ::new(), define PowerShell classes and compile C# with Add-Type.
concepts.why: When no cmdlet exists, the entire .NET library is one line away, and classes give you real types.
concepts.body:
PowerShell runs on .NET, so every .NET type is available. **Static members** use `[Type]::Member`: `[math]::Round(2.567, 2)`, `[System.IO.Path]::GetExtension($f)`, `[datetime]::Parse('2026-01-15')`, `[guid]::NewGuid()`. Common namespaces may be shortened (`[IO.Path]`), and a `using namespace System.Text` line at the top of a script lets you write `[StringBuilder]`. Create instances with `[Type]::new(args)` (or the older `New-Object`).

**PowerShell classes** (since 5.0) define real .NET types with typed properties, constructors, methods, static members, inheritance and enums:

- methods must declare a return type and use `return` explicitly; unlike functions, stray values are **not** output,
- reference the instance with `$this`,
- override `ToString()` to control how objects appear in strings.

Classes are useful for validated data structures and for advanced features like custom validation attributes and DSC resources. Limitations: a class must be defined before the code that uses it is parsed, and changes to a class in a module need a new session to reload.

`Add-Type -TypeDefinition` compiles C# source on the fly, for performance-critical code or P/Invoke calls into native APIs. Compiled types cannot be unloaded from the session, so rename them while iterating.
concepts.code:
[System.IO.Path]::GetExtension('report.final.csv')   # .csv
[math]::Sqrt(144)                                    # 12
[datetime]::Parse('2026-01-15').DayOfWeek            # Thursday
$sb = [System.Text.StringBuilder]::new()
[void]$sb.Append('fast ').Append('strings')
$sb.ToString()                                       # fast strings
class Server {
  [string]$Name
  [int]$Cpu
  Server([string]$name, [int]$cpu) { $this.Name = $name; $this.Cpu = $cpu }
  [bool] IsBusy() { return $this.Cpu -gt 80 }
  [string] ToString() { return "$($this.Name) ($($this.Cpu)%)" }
}
$s = [Server]::new('web1', 92)
$s.IsBusy()                                          # True
"$s"                                                 # web1 (92%)
Add-Type -TypeDefinition 'public static class Calc { public static int Twice(int x) { return x * 2; } }'
[Calc]::Twice(21)                                    # 42
takeaways: [Type]::StaticMember and [Type]::new() reach all of .NET
Class methods need return types and explicit return
Add-Type compiles C# for speed or native interop
pitfalls: Expecting a class method to output values like a function: only the return value comes back.

quiz.q: How do you create a new System.Text.StringBuilder in modern PowerShell?
quiz.explain: ::new() calls the type's constructor; New-Object also works but is slower.

quiz.q: A class method contains `'debug'; return 5`. What does calling it return?
quiz.explain: In class methods only the return statement produces a value; other expressions are discarded.

concepts.name: Output semantics, unrolling and streams
concepts.summary: Why functions return extra values, how collections unroll in the pipeline, and how the six output streams are redirected.
concepts.why: These rules explain the strangest PowerShell bugs: arrays that become scalars and return values with unexpected extra items.
concepts.body:
**Everything uncaptured is output.** `return $x` is just "output $x and leave"; any earlier expression that produced a value, such as a .NET method returning an index (`ArrayList.Add`) or a cmdlet you forgot to silence, is output too, so the caller receives an array. Discard with `$null = ...`, `[void](...)` or `| Out-Null` (the first two are fastest).

**Unrolling**: when a collection is written to the pipeline, it is enumerated item by item. A function returning a one-element array therefore gives the caller a **scalar**, and an empty array gives nothing (`$null`). To return the collection itself, prefix it with the unary comma: `return , $list`. On the caller side, `@(...)` reliably turns any result into an array.

PowerShell has **six streams**: 1 Success (output), 2 Error, 3 Warning, 4 Verbose, 5 Debug, 6 Information. `Write-Host` writes to the Information stream since 5.0, which is why it can now be captured. Redirect by number: `2>&1` merges errors into output, `3> warnings.txt` saves warnings, `*> $null` silences everything, `*>&1` merges all streams into output.

`$null` comparisons also involve this: an empty pipeline result is a special "AutomationNull" that behaves as `$null` but, unlike `$null`, produces no iteration in `foreach`.
concepts.code:
function Get-Two { 'noise'; return 'value' }        # BOTH are output
(Get-Two).Count                                     # 2
function Get-One { return @(42) }
(Get-One).GetType().Name                            # Int32   (unrolled to a scalar)
function Get-Wrapped { return , @(42) }             # unary comma keeps the array
(Get-Wrapped).GetType().Name                        # Object[]
@(Get-One).Count                                    # 1       (@() forces an array)
function Get-None { return @() }
$null -eq (Get-None)                                # True
$al = [System.Collections.ArrayList]::new()
function Add-Item { $al.Add('x'); 'done' }          # Add returns an index...
Add-Item                                            # 0 / done  (leaked output)
$null = $al.Add('y')                                # discard it like this
function Get-Info { Write-Warning 'careful'; Write-Information 'fyi'; 'data' }
$out = Get-Info 3>&1 6>&1                           # merge warning + information
$out.Count                                          # 3
Get-Info *> $null                                   # silence every stream
takeaways: Every uncaptured value is output; return only exits
Collections unroll: return , $arr to keep one, @() to force an array
Streams 1-6; redirect with 2>&1, 3>, *> $null
pitfalls: Calling methods like ArrayList.Add() in a function without discarding the result, so the caller gets extra numbers.

quiz.q: A function ends with `return @('only')`. What type does the caller get?
quiz.explain: The one-element array is unrolled in the pipeline, leaving the single string.

quiz.q: Which redirection silences all streams of a command?
quiz.explain: *> redirects every stream; > and | Out-Null affect only the success stream.

concepts.name: Scopes, dot-sourcing and performance
concepts.summary: How variable scopes work, what $script: and $global: change, and the patterns that make PowerShell code fast.
concepts.why: Scope surprises cause silent bugs, and a few habits make scripts orders of magnitude faster on large data.
concepts.body:
Each script, function and script block runs in its own **scope**. A child scope can **read** variables from its parents, but assigning creates a **new local variable** that hides the parent's one. To change an outer variable, use a scope modifier: `$script:count` (the script's top level) or `$global:count` (the session). `$private:x` hides a variable from child scopes. Modules have their own isolated session state, so their internals do not leak into yours. Dot-sourcing runs a script in the caller's scope instead of a new one.

Usually it is better to **return** values than to modify outer variables; scope modifiers are best kept for module-level state.

Performance habits that matter on large inputs:

- Do not grow arrays with `+=`: assign the output of the loop (`$r = foreach (...) { ... }`) or use `List[T]`.
- The `foreach` **statement** and the `.Where()` / `.ForEach()` methods are much faster than `ForEach-Object` and `Where-Object` for data already in memory; the cmdlets shine for streaming.
- Filter left with cmdlet parameters, and discard output with `$null =` rather than `| Out-Null` in hot loops.
- Build strings with `-join` or a StringBuilder, not repeated `+=`.

Always measure with `Measure-Command { ... }` before and after an optimisation.
takeaways: Assignment creates a local variable; use $script: or $global: deliberately
Capture loop output instead of +=; prefer foreach and .Where() in memory
Measure-Command before and after optimising
pitfalls: Expecting a function's `$total += 1` to update the script's $total.

quiz.q: A script sets $n = 1; a function runs `$n = 5`. What is $n at script level afterwards?
quiz.explain: Assignment in the function creates a local $n; the script's variable is untouched.

quiz.q: Which builds a 100,000-item result fastest?
quiz.explain: Assigning the loop's output collects items once; += copies the whole array on every iteration.
